Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally strained: intense guilt, rage, and overwhelming grief on recall can co-occur, but selecting all three as core recall responses without any memory-content item suggests an over-broad affect cluster rather than a coherent memory profile.

Cross-node coherence is weak between Negative Appraisals and Memory: 'No Accountability' aligns with anger/rage, but 'Contamination' is more typical of sexual trauma or morally violating trauma and is not well supported by the rest of the assault profile.

For an adult male assaulted in a non-sexual assault profile, 'Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is clinically hard to reconcile unless other items indicate sexual assault, bodily violation, or washing/avoidance themes, which are absent here.

For an adult male assault survivor, intense guilt, overwhelming grief, and feeling dirty/contaminated can occur, but this specific combination is hard to reconcile without any accompanying sexual-assault-type cues elsewhere in the profile. The contamination appraisal in particular pulls toward a trauma meaning not supported by the other selected items.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' and 'Grief on Recall' are not contradictory, but paired with predominantly visual memories they imply a complex emotional recall profile that would usually be echoed in appraisals more directly tied to guilt/loss. Instead, the appraisal set emphasizes injustice, incapacity, and contamination, which do not form a tight thematic cluster.

The formulation has a strong Negative Appraisals → Threat link, so appraisals should plausibly explain the threat items. 'No Longer Capable' fits hypervigilance/feeling unsafe, but 'No Accountability' mainly reflects injustice and does not clearly drive 'Safe Zone Only' or 'Startle to Movement.' 'Contamination' especially does not map well to the selected threat items, making the appraisal-to-threat pattern clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, Self-Blame and No Accountability point in different directions of responsibility for the assault. A patient can feel both guilt and anger, but stated this strongly they suggest opposing appraisals about who is responsible.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences
issues.explanation: Memory item Guilt on Recall reinforces self-blame, which increases the inconsistency with the concurrent appraisal that perpetrators are the ones who should face consequences. The profile mixes strong perpetrator-focused blame with strong self-focused blame without a coherent bridge in the selected items.

The negative appraisal items are dominated by external blame/injustice ('the people responsible have faced no consequences', 'what happened was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it'), which fits an assault survivor, but this sits poorly with 'When I remember the event I feel intense guilt.' Intense guilt usually implies some degree of self-blame, responsibility, or perceived preventability. While mixed emotions are possible, this combination is clinically hard to reconcile here because the appraisal node contains no corresponding self-blaming belief and instead consistently locates responsibility outside the patient.

Within the Memory node, 'Guilt on Recall' is not well aligned with the other memory qualities selected ('mostly pictures or images' and 'can't put the event into words'), which describe sensory, poorly elaborated trauma memory. Those memory-form items plausibly link to threat, but guilt-on-recall points to a different meaning structure that is not supported by the selected negative appraisals. Given the formulation's strongest active pathway is Negative Appraisals → Threat, the absence of guilt-based appraisals makes the guilt memory item feel disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Adebayo was a 50-year-old married plumber who had built his life around being dependable, physically capable, and calm in tight spaces. He described that before the assault he moved through his work with confidence, carrying tools into basements, crawl spaces, and back rooms without much thought. That changed after an evening in which he was attacked by another man in circumstances that still felt, to him, senseless and unresolved. He did not linger on every detail of the event in words; when he tried to tell it, he became stuck at the level of images. What remained most vivid were sudden pictures: the other man too close, the violence arriving before he could prepare, the body memory of being overpowered. Even now, when he recalled it, he felt a surge of guilt that sat beside the memory like a weight, and he kept returning to the feeling that he should have done something differently, though he could not settle on exactly what. He said the event felt deeply unfair, and what troubled him as much as the assault itself was that nothing had been done about it. The lack of any clear reckoning left him with the sense that the wrong had simply been allowed to stand.

In the months that followed, Adebayo found that his world had narrowed. He said he only felt safe in a very limited number of places, and he began organizing his days around those few spaces that felt predictable: his home, a particular seat in the church hall, and the driver’s side of his van when he was parked outside a job. Everywhere else carried a thin but constant edge of danger. At work, the places that once felt routine now took effort to enter. If a call required him to kneel behind a water heater in a cramped utility room or reach into a dim basement corner, he did it, but he did so with a tension that never quite left him. Sudden movement nearby was especially hard. If a homeowner stepped quickly into the garage, if a coworker came up behind him without warning, or if a child darted past in a hallway, Adebayo would jerk back as though the danger were immediate and physical. He knew these reactions were disproportionate, yet in the moment his body seemed to move before his thoughts did.

Sleep became difficult as well. He had trouble falling asleep and often woke in the night, lying in the dark with his mind alert for reasons he could not fully name. On those nights he would turn over and over, listening to every small sound in the house, knowing his wife was nearby yet still unable to settle. He had become careful in a way that extended beyond the bedroom. He avoided places that were not part of the small circle he had come to trust, and this had consequences that showed up in daily life. He declined some social invitations, took longer routes when traveling, and found himself less willing to accept jobs that would place him in unfamiliar buildings or neighborhoods. For a man who had once defined himself through competence and movement, that shrinking of his range felt humiliating. He said, with a flatness that carried real grief, that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him. It was not only about strength; it was about the version of himself who had once entered any space and felt able to manage it.

When he did think about the assault, he rarely experienced it as a story with a beginning, middle, and end. It arrived instead as fragments, mostly pictures or images, and he struggled to translate those fragments into words. He would start to explain and then stop, saying that the event sat in his mind like a scene he could see but not properly speak. The images were made worse by the guilt he felt on recall, because each picture seemed to carry the accusation that he ought to have prevented what happened. That self-doubt has become one of the hardest parts of his current life. He now finds himself questioning whether he can trust himself to do the right thing, even in ordinary situations. He hesitates before making decisions at work, second-guesses himself in conversations, and notices the hesitation with frustration. His wife has urged him for some time to talk to someone, but he delayed until the changes had become impossible to ignore. What finally brought him in was the accumulation of all these things: the sleeping problems, the constant need to stay within a narrow safe zone, the startle reactions that embarrassed him, and the heavy conviction that what happened to him was unjust and unresolved. He came to treatment hoping to feel steadier again, but he also admitted that what he most feared was discovering that he would never fully trust himself, or feel like the man who used to move through the world without bracing for the next unexpected movement.
